Your Honours, I've tried to finish within the six hours you gave me yesterday, and I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I have to admit I'm a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you commence your re-examination, Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a small one for my education and for the witness. Can you tell me exactly when the Republika Srpska came into being? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an Assembly session where it was proclaimed. And its first name was the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then the name was changed, either in late 1992 or early 1993, into the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, now it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. President. I was about to say I'm caught a little off guard. I do have material that I'd like to examine the witness on, but the material is still upstairs. So it might be a good idea, since it's 10 minutes before the break, if you could give me -- if we could take the break now, I'll get the material and then I'll -- and then I can commence the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a very good proposal. We should have our second break now, and we will resume 10 minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours. And good afternoon to you, Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We haven't met, and as you know, I'm here in place of Mr. McCloskey. But I do have a few questions with respect to your cross-examination that I'd like to put to you. During the cross-examination, at least today, and I think part of yesterday too, many questions were put to you where General Tolimir asked you about information that "we" had, "we" in the plural sense, which I took to mean you and General Tolimir. First, can you tell me, is that a fair understanding of what you meant when you responded to his questions concerning information that "we" had?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- when we co-operated together. Do you refer to our co-operation in preparing some of the reports? Yes, where he was abreast of the contents, and he was my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned during your examination -- on cross-examination that General Tolimir was the sector chief for intelligence and security and therefore determined what information went to the Security Administration and the Intelligence Administration within the Main Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Intelligence Administration was drafting the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But as the sector chief, General Tolimir received certain information that you didn't necessarily receive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was receiving information from the other service as well, the Security Service, and he could then tell them, Yes, forward the information, the intelligence, to the Intelligence Administration, or the other way around. If we had information that would be of interest to the Security Service, we would forward that to them. Yes, he was the one co-ordinating that, and also to the other end users. He would determine who is to get which piece of intelligence, depending on the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for clarifying that. Now, you mentioned during your cross-examination -- or you were asked, rather, with respect to certain code-names; do you recall that? In particular about the code-name Uran.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think you indicated that you did not know what that code-name stood for or represented.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, that's at page 13612 of the transcript. I'd like to show you 65 ter 5271, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what you should have here is a document from the Drina Corps Command, dated the 11 July 1995, and it's sent to the Special Police Brigade Command, concerning code signs for Krivaja-95. And I think you're familiar with what Krivaja-95 was about, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the name of the operation, Krivaja-95.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is show you page 2 of this in English and in B/C/S. There, you can see, where it says "Plan" or "Rada," the work plan for this operation, Krivaja-95, and you can see that the first line, the first entry, says: "Drina Corps IKM." Do you see that? It's on the left-hand side in the top corner.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then you can see the code-name that applies to that as "Uran."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then you can see a number of code-names for other units.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this kind of assigning of code-names was typical and normal for the conduct of any given operation, in your experience, in the military; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For operations, one would develop a communications plan, which would be done, normally, by the chief of the Communications Sector and the operative officer. But in times of war, code-names are used all the time; even in peacetime, sometimes. Military phone and radio communications normally avoid naming the 1st Brigade, 1st Division, or this or that. Instead, they use, for instance, "Uran," or a commander would have his call sign, for instance, 100. So one wouldn't ask for the commander, but, Give me number 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that explanation, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document. It's 5271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P2208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness another document. This is another document with a code-name on it. Mr. President, this one, I don't think -- this is a document that I think I need to apply to the Trial Chamber to use. It was not on the Prosecution's original 65 ter list. Its number is 7352.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is not on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's not on the 65 ter -- original 65 ter exhibit list; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, Colonel, are you familiar with this document? Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the code-name that is indicated at the top, where it reads "Klej"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about the two following code-names, one named Rada and then a source named Pilot? --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with the code-names in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just to give you a little bit of background, this was a document that was recovered amongst other documents in a folder, related to an individual code-named Atlantida. First, are you familiar with that code-name? And to put it in context, in relation to the events in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with "Atlantida." I apologise. I just wanted to say that at the period I did not take part in any planning or any activities related to the operation. I was in my office at the time, yes, but I stayed there, and I was not involved in any activities. I was not privy to code-names or code signals, nor did I have any communication with anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you about one thing that's in this document. If we go to the second page in the English, and I think it's just at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, it reads that: "Krsto and Peric met in Bijeljina with Generals Ratko Mladic and Zdravko Tolimir and familiarised them with the collected material on the fall of Western Slavonia and the persons guilty of everything that happened there." Are you familiar, first of all, with the fall -- the circumstances surrounding the fall of Western Slavonia, which I'm sure you must be? And if you are, are you familiar with the circumstances concerning this meeting in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Slavonia, yes. That was the first Croatian offensive against forces of the Republika Srpska in one of the UNPA areas. The code-name of that operation was -- just give me a second. The other one was Storm. I can't remember the name of this one. And it was completed in a very short period, extremely quickly. The Croats took the area, took control of the area. People and the troops from the area crossed over to the territory of Republika Srpska at the Gradiska Bridge, and then they were received. Most of them went on to Serbia later on. I think this was late autumn, but I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you can see this document, in particular, is dated --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 1994. And let me just add -- but, no, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This document is dated 16 July 1995. Can you tell us anything about this meeting between General Mladic and General Tolimir in Bijeljina? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it for the first time now. This is the first time I am made aware of any such meeting, my first contact with such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just so that I'm clear, it is the first time you've seen the document, but it's also the first time you've ever heard that there was a meeting that occurred around that date?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, absolutely. This is the first information I have about such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I don't see that this witness testified about the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I see that he's not familiar with it. I don't know whether or not the Defence can test the authenticity of the document, but it does relate, I think, to a salient issue in the case. It relates to the whereabouts of General Tolimir on the 16th of July, which I think is quite important. And to the extent -- to the extent that the Defence doesn't object to its authenticity, I would propose to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document does not state that Tolimir was on the location on the 16th. This is the date when Klej interrogated Pilot and compiled and sent the document to Rada, but we do not know anything about when the activities described therein took place. And maybe Mr. Salapura can help there. General Rupert Smith, in his testimony, said that General Mladic was in Belgrade on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know whether or not that's an objection to the admission of the document. If the witness has a recollection as to the specific events, which is what I thought I asked him, yeah, then I would like to know if he has a recollection of this meeting, and, if he does, when he recalls that it took place. That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. I didn't know about this meeting at all. I don't know anything about the content. I don't know that such a meeting was held in Bijeljina. A meeting attended by General Mladic and Tolimir; this is what I am reading from the document. I don't know who Krsto is. I don't know of this Peric. I know of one Peric, Slobodan Peric. I think he was a colonel who was in the area of Western Slavonia. I think he was a commander, even, but that's all I know. It's the first time I see this document and that I've heard of such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will only be marked for identification. It may be used with another witness, but it will not be admitted into evidence because this witness couldn't say anything about the content and the source and the authenticity. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be P2209, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show the witness P112 -- 1112, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have in front of you, Colonel, is an instruction. It's issued, as you can see, on the 24th of October, 1994, from the Main Staff of the VRS, and it is signed for the commander, General Mladic. You'll see, in the course of these instructions, under item 1, for example, he talks about the field of work of the security and intelligence organs, and he talks about intelligence and security tasks and the way they should be divided up as per this instruction. What I wanted to show you -- first of all, are you familiar with this instruction?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I would have to read it, and then maybe based on the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just ask you a little about it, then. In the first item, it reads that: "The field of work of the VRS security and intelligence organ primarily includes intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks ..." That's consistent with your testimony so far; right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean, I'm not contending any of this. I'm just saying that I don't remember having read that. Thousands of documents went through my hands, and this is almost 20 years ago. And I just don't have the capacity to keep it all in my head all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sure, sure. That's understandable. Let me take you to item number 6, which is at page 3 in the English, and it should be page 3 in the B/C/S. Item 6 reads that: "All security and intelligence organs," and it says "and unit and institution command organs are obliged to provide every assistance in their operative work and tasks to the detached and deployed organs of the 410th Intelligence Centre and Counter-Intelligence Group of the VRS." Now, you've mentioned the 410th Intelligence Centre. Let me just ask: Is this paragraph accurate; that is, were security and intelligence organs and institutional command organs obliged to provide assistance to the 410th Intelligence Centre?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may elaborate, please. The 410th Intelligence Centre had its points throughout the territory of Republika Srpska, from Trebinje to Novi Grad, and this instruction that was signed by General Tolimir, because I think this is his signature, because this is a group of people, two or three of them, who were in charge of the operative intelligence. They had a specific room dedicated to them, but they had various problems related to fuel supply, logistics supplies of all sorts. They were independent in the area. They were directly under their chief of centre who was in Banja Luka, but they were within the areas of responsibility of various units. The same situation was with a counter-intelligence group, and that's why General Tolimir had to draft this. And we see that this was something he signed upon commander's authority, and then he sent this document to the corps, asking for such assistance to be provided to these men in order to make their -- to facilitate their work and to enable them to use the corps' communications systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would their work be facilitated, for example, by providing them with continuous and accurate intelligence information or security information?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, as far as the intelligence segment is concerned, yes, yes, they were receiving reports or information, because they co-operated with the officer -- intelligence officer in the corps command. For instance, if you had their point in Trebinje, they would be in touch with the intelligence organ of the relevant corps command. They had authority to provide any information or intelligence relevant to that corps immediately to the intelligence officer of the corps, in other words, to avoid sending it first from there to Banja Luka, then to Han Pijesak, and then back to them. These organs were not integral parts of the corps. They were not under the command of the corps commander. And the purpose of this document is to increase efficiency. Likewise, the intelligence organs of the corps who are immediately subordinated to the chief of staff of the corps, this document authorises them or tasks them or approves their exchange of information with the other group. I don't know whether you've understood me fully. I hope I've been clear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I think I have. And I'd like to direct your attention to the next paragraph, which reads that: "The monitoring of the professionalism, legality, and correctness of the work of the security and intelligence organs shall be carried out exclusively by the first superior organs for security and intelligence affairs, except in that part of their engagement relating to command and staff affairs." I just want to ask you, very simply, whether or not that is an accurate -- whether or not that accurately applies to your recollection of how things functioned during 1995 and other relevant periods of time.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how things should be all the time, from the beginning of the war until the very end. During that period, the chief of sector who worked with both services noticed certain problems, and that's why he intervened with the commander, asking him to issue this document in order to remove all those problems. Nothing special was done here. This is the principle of functioning and subordination within different services. Maybe this applies more to the Security Service and the organs of the 410th Intelligence Centre. When it comes to the 410th Security Centre, they did not deal with staff duties in the staff, whereas the Intelligence Services are, but they don't engage in operative intelligence work, whereas all intelligence services deal with intelligence and counter-intelligence duties. When it comes to the professional level of work, it is the superior officer along the security line that is in charge of them. And the staff duties, it would be the chief of staff or the commander. When it comes to intelligence organs, the intelligence organ in the corps is subordinated to the chief of staff of the corps. I was not the one who was in charge of them, nor was it the Intelligence Administration. He is subordinated to the corps, and he reports to them. And the organs of the 410th Intelligence Centre, as I've already told you, even those ones who are detached and in the areas of different responsibility, they were subordinated to the chief of centre in Banja Luka, whereas the latter is subordinated to me. However, they do not participate in the work either of the corps command or in their staff duties. They just exchanged information. I don't know if I have made myself clear to -- if not, I am willing to continue in order to make things even clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You made it clear. I want to ask, very simply: In principle, is it or was it the case that the first superior organs for security and intelligence were responsible for monitoring the professionalism, legality, and correctness of the work of security/intelligence organs, as you can see is written in this document signed for General Mladic by General Tolimir? Was that the case? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the case. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see this document was MFI'd. I'd like to have it admitted at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would not deal with the issue. Just for the record, there will be some problems with the translation of the document and the use of terminology. However, we will deal with that when the time comes, hopefully very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have another document that was not on the original 65 ter list. It's another document that concerns the 410th Intelligence Centre that the witness testified to, which I would like to show him, because it also relates to the intelligence and security organs of the Main Staff, which was the subject of his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please give us the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry. It's 65 ter 7363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could please have that shown to the witness. This is a document dated 10 April 1994. It's issued from the Main Staff. And if we go to the last -- I think it's the last page. Yes, it's the last page in the B/C/S, and I think the third page in the English. We can see that this was signed by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At that time, Colonel Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's page 2 in the B/C/S. All right, I think we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You can see that, Colonel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. This is an order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll have to go to the first page in both documents, I think. First, let me just note who this is directed to. And it says that it's directed to the intelligence section of the corps. It's also sent to the Main Staff Counter-Intelligence Group; that's the "KOG" that we referred to previously. And also to the 410th Intelligence Centre, which we saw on the other document. If we go to the second page in the English, we can also see that it's sent to the 27th Logistical Base, the 30th, 35th Logistical Bases. And it says that: "With a view to improve a more efficient organisation of the security and intelligence organs of the Army of Republika Srpska," which you were just talking about, "and faster and more efficient exchange of information and co-ordination in the execution of jobs and tasks which fall within the remit of intelligence and security organs, I issue the following order:" Now, what I'd like to do is refer you to some specific provisions in this order. If we go to paragraph 4, which starts on the first page of the B/C/S, we can see that it says: "Intelligence and security organs of the Main Staff," "Glavni Staba Vojska," "will be directed subordinated to the OB Sector of the Main Staff. They will send security and intelligence reports to the Security and/or Intelligence Section of the OB Sector by telegram or regular mail."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, having been there at the time, first, are you familiar with this order? And, secondly, if you are familiar with the order, was it implemented, as is indicated here, or in the terms that it's indicated here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember the contents of this order. It was implemented, and maybe you would like to hear my comment in order to understand things better. I already spoke about that during the examination-in-chief, when I was answering Mr. McCloskey's questions, when we spoke about that. The intelligence element was short-staffed. There were very few professionals working in the Intelligence Service. Bosnia and Herzegovina was in the depth of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. There were no intelligence institutions that would be dealing with operative work. The units were very small, and they did not have intelligence organs; very few in peacetime. When the war started, only very few of us, perhaps four or five, in the entire VRS were active servicemen dealing with that. That's one of the reasons, and that's one of the things that you need to understand. Secondly, why was this drafted in the first place? At the corps level, for a time we -- let me explain. I believe that it was an organisational issue, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fair. The reason I'm trying to move on is because I'm a bit pressed for time, so I just need your answers, if possible, to be responsive to the question. And that is: Was this implemented during the time that you were the chief of the Intelligence Administration in the Main Staff? That's all.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was implemented. However, there is a clause here which was not implemented. The intelligence organs were tied to another administration along the professional lines. They were not subordinated to the Intelligence Administration. They were subordinated to the chief of the corps, not to the chief of the Intelligence Administration. And the same applied to the security organs who were subordinated to the commander. For a while, at the corps level we had a Department for Intelligence and Security, up to 1994, and then that was split. The two were divided into the security and intelligence. And the more people joined the Intelligence Service, the more gradually the separation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Under paragraph 4, it says that: "The intelligence and security organs of the Main Staff will be directly subordinated to the Sector of Intelligence and Security for the Main Staff." That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In practice, that never happened, nor was it possible. The intelligence organs in the corps were an element of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the corps. Just try and follow my question.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Main Staff, oh, oh, okay. The Main Staff, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I'd like to have this document admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also says, in paragraph 5, that: "All intelligence and security organs of the Army of Republika Srpska will send their security and intelligence reports to the Security or Intelligence Section of the Security and intelligence Sector indicating whether it deals with intelligence or counter-intelligence issues." That's right too, isn't it? I see you nodding, but you have to answer.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this relates to the witness's prior testimony concerning Dragomir Pecanac. I don't have the specific cite, but it related to the witness's testimony concerning Mr. Pecanac's -- or his familiarity with Mr. Pecanac's position in the Main Staff. The 65 ter number of the document, I'm sorry, is 7365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, if you're asking for that, to add it to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry. If I could have that shown to the witness as well. All right. If we could just focus on the very top right corner of the document. That's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can see here that this is a document that's issued from the Intelligence Centre. It's a bit distorted at the top, but you can see it says "1-3/410."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I apologise, Mr. President. I don't think we have a translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But it says "Obavestenje Centar." That's the Intelligence Centre, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. That's how I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's dated 29 June 1995. I'd just like to --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 29th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'd just like to take you to the last page of this document. I see that it's taking a little while, but what you'll see on the last page of the document is that it's signed by Dragomir Pecanac, and it says "Captain First Class, Nacelnik," "Chief." Can you tell us what your recollection is of Mr. Pecanac's position with respect to the 410th Intelligence Centre?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Pecanac, I believe that at the time he was a member of the 410th Intelligence Centre, for a while, at least, but I don't know for how long. I can't help you with that. And then in the month of June he was the head of General Mladic's office. General Mladic requested him to join his office as the head of office. And in the month of June -- I don't know exactly when that happened, I don't know on what date, but -- or perhaps in May, or March, or June. Sometime. In any case, at that time I don't believe that he was in the 410th Intelligence Centre, on the 23rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And the --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can check that for you. I can give you the exact date when he left the Intelligence Centre and joined General Mladic's office as head of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. That would be helpful. I don't think we can do it today, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document, as it is relevant to the position that was held by Captain Pecanac during the relevant period. And I have another document I'd like to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura -- oh, it is gone. I would like to have the last page back. My question would be if you recognise this signature, which seems to be the signature of Mr. Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recognise it. I did not see his signature that often. It says here that it's his signature, but I cannot be of assistance to you. I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This document will be received as an exhibit. It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2211, MFI, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We just lost what we had on the screen, and I don't want to put it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But did you see on the screen that that document was copied to the Intelligence Administration of the Main Staff? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another document I'd like to show the witness. It's 7364. And again, Mr. President, this was a document that was not on the Prosecution's original 65 ter list, but it relates specifically to the intelligence about the enclaves Gorazde, Zepa and Srebrenica, which were clearly the subject matter of the witness's cross-examination. It's also a document that was written by Dragomir Pecanac, emanating from the 410th Intelligence Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 410th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Here we see a document dated 28th May, 1995. It is an intelligence report, and it concerns a number of intelligence information -- not a number, a large amount of intelligence information concerning the Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica enclaves. And as I indicated, it is signed by -- submitted by Captain Pecanac. If we go to the last page, we can see that. All right. What I wanted to do was focus your attention very briefly on page 7 in the B/C/S, page 13 in the English, and it concerns intelligence on the Zepa enclave. And if you can see that there, it provides the area of the enclave, the population here indicated, 7.000 to 8.000, indication that it's densely populated. It tells us about the refugee camps, topical characteristics. We have to go to the next page in the B/C/S. It talks about areas in which people can take shelter, such as a large number of caves and depressions. We have to go to the next page in the English, too. And then if we go to page 21 in the English and page 12 in the B/C/S, we will see similar information concerning the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question to you is: This is information that was -- that came from the 410th Intelligence Centre which I assume that you received. First, can you tell us, did you receive this type of information from the 410th Intelligence Centre regarding the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I believe that he used information that the Intelligence Department of the Drina Corps had. They had such detailed and elaborated intelligence study for Srebrenica and Zepa. I believe that this was taken from there, that Pecanac took that study from there and used it. They were not in charge of either receiving or disseminating such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Where would a report like this go? To whom would Pecanac have sent this report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the chief of the 410th Centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And wouldn't you --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the letter should have been forwarded to us in the Main Staff. However, what I'm saying is that I'm familiar with the content of this report, and what I'm saying also is that he took it from the Intelligence Department of the Drina Corps. I don't know whether he forwarded the study to somebody else. It is not his study. It doesn't emanate from him. He took it from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So let me just ask this as briefly as I can. From what I understand of what you're saying is that the source of the information may have come from the Drina Corps, but that the information, as acquired by Mr. Pecanac, would have been sent to the Main Staff of the VRS. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff already had those information, those reports. We received them from the Drina Corps. I don't know whether Pecanac took their information and then copied it and sent it again. Maybe he just took the report for his own files, because the Drina Corps was keeping meticulously all the informations about Srebrenica and Zepa. They had more information and more detailed information than the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well as for Gorazde, yes, for that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I know, Mr. President. To be honest, I can't finish him in the time I've got left. I've got --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you can't, we can't [Realtime transcript read in error "can"] continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think I'm recorded incorrectly. We can't continue, and we shouldn't continue. What is your estimation about the remainder of the examination-in-chief -- re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have about five more documents to go through, and I'm moving at a relatively slow pace. I think almost the same amount of time as I've taken now, but I can try and whittle it down some before we get started next week, because I don't want to gum up the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was hoping that we could finish with this witness today, which means this week, but this seems not to be possible. So we have to adjourn for the week and to resume on Monday, 2.15 in the afternoon, in this courtroom, Courtroom III. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
